headline: CNN says a US-Saudi nuclear deal under congressional review gives the kingdom a conditional path to enrich uranium at home; the agreement Trump sent to Congress (H. Doc. 119-191) matches
claim: "A nuclear deal between the US and the Saudis currently under congressional review would provide a pathway for the kingdom to enrich uranium on its own soil if specific conditions, including US approval, are met." — CNN, Davis Winkie, Nov. 7, 2026
record_title: House Document 119-191, Communication from the President transmitting the U.S.-Saudi Arabia Agreement for Cooperation Concerning Peaceful Uses of Nuclear Energy (Sec. 123, Atomic Energy Act), referred to House Foreign Affairs Aug. 27, 2026
why: House Document 119-191 shows the agreement was formally transmitted to Congress and referred to the House Foreign Affairs Committee on Aug. 27, 2026, starting the Atomic Energy Act's 90-day continuous-session review, which had not run out by Nov. 7. The transmittal says the deal would permit sensitive nuclear technology transfers to support a joint enrichment and conversion study or upon written agreement of the parties, and the Arms Control Association's review of the text says enrichment may occur only if the parties agree in writing after that study, starting at 5 percent. That is a conditional pathway requiring U.S. consent, as CNN says.
what_would_change: A passed joint resolution of disapproval, the review period ending so the deal enters into force, or a release of the classified side letters showing enrichment without U.S. consent would move this verdict.
outlet: CNN, Davis Winkie, “60 years of denial about Israel’s nuclear weapons program confronts a new reality,” Nov. 7, 2026
script: Midday Check. CNN says a US-Saudi nuclear deal under congressional review would give the kingdom a path to enrich uranium at home if conditions, including US approval, are met. script:
Good evening, I'm Professor Reid, and this is ReFrame. Tonight... NBC News reports: Democrat Haley Stevens endorses Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan Senate race two days before Election Day.
NBC News reported this on November 1.
The headline: Democrat Haley Stevens endorses Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan Senate race two days before Election Day.
Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost Michigan's Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed Republican nominee Mike Rogers on Sunday after appearing with him at a Detroit church service.
In a video she said El-Sayed had told her she was no longer welcome in his campaign and that she does not stand with streamer Hasan Piker, who has appeared with El-Sayed.
Let's grade the headline.
Argument one. It comes from Rep. Haley Stevens.
The reasons. Reason one. Abdul El-Sayed said she was no longer welcome in his campaign and should stay away.
Reason two. El-Sayed has campaigned with streamer Hasan Piker, and she does not stand with Piker or with hate.
Reason three. An unstated reason, one we supply: If she can't support El-Sayed, the only remaining choice is to back his Republican opponent.
Therefore... She is endorsing Republican Mike Rogers for the US Senate.
Here's the question worth asking. If Stevens can't campaign for Abdul El-Sayed, why does that mean endorsing Mike Rogers rather than staying neutral?
Valid? No.
Cogent? No.
Supported? Partly.
Any fallacies? Yes. Two: false dilemma, and guilt by association.
That's a D-plus.
The first fallacy in argument one... false dilemma.
Here's the line. Quote... Abdul said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign... and he's right, and that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers.
Why does it fail here? Being unwelcome in one campaign leaves more than one option: she could stay neutral or simply decline to campaign. Stepping away from El-Sayed does not by itself lead to endorsing his opponent.
The second fallacy in argument one... guilt by association.
Here's the line. Quote... We can't stand with hate. We can't stand with Hasan Piker.
Why does it fail here? It judges El-Sayed by a streamer who appeared with him. NPR reports El-Sayed said Piker does not speak for his campaign, though he stopped short of disavowing him. Piker's remarks are not evidence about El-Sayed's own positions.
*On screen only (grader's comment, verbatim): "The campaign did ask her to stay away, NBC confirms that much. But that, plus a guest who appeared at his events, doesn't get you to endorsing the other party's nominee. And days earlier she said she'd back the ticket; pressed on CNN about what changed, she didn't point to anything specific."*
*Reid speaks a gentler paraphrase (persona: no insults):*
Why D plus? The campaign did ask her to stay away, NBC confirms that much.
Put plainly, and kindly: the conclusion reaches further than the reasons can carry; only some of it is shown, and false dilemma and guilt by association stand in for the missing steps. A more modest claim would earn a better grade.
And days earlier she said she'd back the ticket; pressed on CNN about what changed, she didn't point to anything specific.
Argument two. It comes from Michigan Democratic Party chair Curtis Hertel.
The reasons. Reason one. Stevens chose to campaign with Mike Rogers.
Reason two. Hertel says Rogers wants a national abortion ban and has pledged to be a loyal vote for Trump's agenda.
Reason three. An unstated reason, one we supply: Backing a candidate who opposes some of your positions means you have given up all of them.
Therefore... Stevens has abandoned everything she claims to care about.
Valid? No.
Cogent? No.
Supported? Partly.
Any fallacies? Yes. One: hasty generalization.
That's a C-minus.
The fallacy in argument two... hasty generalization.
Here's the line. Quote... Shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about.
Why does it fail here? One endorsement is stretched into a verdict on every position she holds. Stevens says she still believes in everything she voted for; Hertel's statement offers nothing beyond the endorsement to show otherwise.
Why C minus? A party chair is entitled to call the move disloyal, and the claims about Rogers are his characterization, not something the article checks.
The leap is from one vote in one race to 'everything she claims to care about.'
Argument three. It comes from NBC News.
The reasons. Reason one. Stevens endorsed Rogers in a video after appearing with him at a Detroit church, Rogers' spokesperson confirmed.
Reason two. Michigan's Senate race is one of the most competitive and could help decide which party controls the Senate.
Reason three. Her chief of staff and other staff are resigning, and Democratic leaders condemned the move.
Therefore... Stevens' endorsement is a major shake-up in the final stages of a top battleground race.
Valid? Yes.
Cogent? Yes.
Supported? Yes.
Any fallacies? None found.
That's a B-plus.
Why B plus? The facts are quoted and attributed, and both campaigns were asked for comment.
'Major shake-up' describes the turmoil, not the result: NBC itself says it's unclear how much the endorsement will change the outcome, with more than 2 million votes already cast.
Now, the whole scorecard. Every term here is explained in our grading legend, How We Rate.
Valid: 33 percent.
Cogent: 33 percent.
Conclusion supported: 67 percent.
Fallacy-free: 40 percent.
Overall... a C-plus.
In one line: NBC's account is well sourced and gives both sides; the weakest reasoning in the story is Stevens' own case for backing Rogers, and Democrats' 'abandoned everything' reply overreaches too.
Three arguments. One valid. One cogent. One fully supported. Three fallacies.
Don't just read the news. ReFrame it.

Graded B overall across 3 arguments. US District Judge Trina Thompson: A-. The Trump administration (Justice Department and DHS, as relayed by CNN): C-. CNN (reporter Tierney Sneed): B+. why: The judge's reasoning follows: if processing ballots as the law requires is lawful, threats to prosecute that work have no legal footing, though it is a temporary order on a 'likely' standard and the DOJ has appealed. script:
Good evening, I'm Professor Reid, and this is ReFrame. Tonight... CNN reports: Judge blocks DOJ threats to prosecute election workers over noncitizen voter lists days before the midterms.
CNN reported this on October 30.
The headline: Judge blocks DOJ threats to prosecute election workers over noncitizen voter lists days before the midterms.
US District Judge Trina Thompson granted a temporary restraining order Friday barring the Justice Department and DHS from threatening, intimidating or coercing election officials over voters the administration alleges are noncitizens.
While the order is in place, the agencies cannot demand that officials in any state segregate ballots, purge voters or halt ballot processing, and must tell officials who got warning letters that those threats are blocked.
The order runs to November 16; the DOJ appealed on Saturday.
Let's grade the headline.
Argument one. It comes from US District Judge Trina Thompson.
The reasons. Reason one. When election workers distribute, process or count ballots as state and federal election laws require, they do not violate federal criminal law, even if a particular ballot belongs to a registered voter the administration alleges is ineligible.
Reason two. The Justice Department threatened election workers with criminal prosecution for processing such ballots and demanded that officials segregate ballots, remove voters or halt processing.
Reason three. An unstated reason, one we supply: Threatening prosecution for lawful election work, weeks before an election, intimidates the people running it.
Therefore... The administration's actions are likely to interfere with election administration and disenfranchise lawful voters, so they must stop while the case proceeds.
Valid? Yes.
Cogent? Yes.
Supported? Yes.
Any fallacies? None found.
That's an A-minus.
Why A minus? The reasoning follows: if the work itself is lawful, threats to prosecute it have no legal footing.
It is a temporary order on a 'likely' standard, not a final ruling, and the DOJ has appealed, so the last word isn't in yet.
Argument two. It comes from the Trump administration. The reporter relays it... and does not adopt it.
The reasons. Reason one. DHS compared state voter lists with federal records and produced lists of people it alleges are noncitizens.
Reason two. Election workers who process ballots cast by noncitizens could face criminal prosecution.
Reason three. An unstated reason, one we supply: Being on the DHS list shows that a voter is a noncitizen.
Therefore... Election officials should segregate, refuse or stop processing the ballots of voters on those lists, and the actions are designed to halt unlawful voting by noncitizens.
Here's the question worth asking. If the DHS lists include US citizens, how does setting aside every ballot on them stop only illegal votes?
Valid? Yes.
Cogent? No.
Supported? Partly.
Any fallacies? None found.
That's a C-minus.
Why C minus? The argument only works if the list is accurate, and that is the weak link: election officials say the lists are unreliable and include US citizens, and the 9th Circuit already said the administration can't step in on how states verify citizenship.
A list of suspected noncitizens is a lead to check, not proof.
Argument three. It comes from CNN.
The reasons. Reason one. The order bars the DOJ and DHS from making these demands of election officials in any state, not just California.
Reason two. Several judges are scrutinizing the DHS approach, and the 9th Circuit rejected the administration's demands in California.
Therefore... The judge imposed a sweeping emergency order, and the administration's aggressive efforts have increasingly run aground in the courts.
Valid? Yes.
Cogent? Yes.
Supported? Yes.
Any fallacies? None found.
That's a B-plus.
Why B plus? 'Sweeping' fits an order that reaches every state, and CNN quotes the order directly.
Words like 'pressure campaign' and 'aggressive' are CNN's own characterizations, and the DOJ's side appears only as its stated goal and a note that it was asked for comment.
Now, the whole scorecard. Every term here is explained in our grading legend, How We Rate.
Valid: 100 percent.
Cogent: 67 percent.
Conclusion supported: 83 percent.
Fallacy-free: 100 percent.
Overall... a B.
In one line: CNN's account of the ruling is well sourced to the order itself; the judge's legal reasoning holds up, while the administration's case rests on lists that election officials say include US citizens.
Three arguments. Three valid. Two cogent. Two fully supported. Zero fallacies.
Don't just read the news. ReFrame it.

read: The attribution is relayed with care; the AI angle is a guess riding on a laundering quote. Graded C+ overall across 3 arguments. TRM Labs and Chainalysis, relayed by the BBC: B. Lily Jamali, BBC North America Technology correspondent, on AI being used to break in: D (non sequitur). Lily Jamali on how powerful North Korea's hackers have become: B-. Scorecard: 0% valid, 67% cogent, 33% supported, 80% fallacy-free.
why: The North Korea attribution is well sourced: TRM Labs and Chainalysis both name TraderTraitor (Lazarus) "with high confidence", and the BBC keeps it conditional, but the article never shows their evidence; Chainalysis's own write-up cites stolen Binance funds commingling on-chain with funds from the September Bitget theft. The claim that AI was plausibly used to infiltrate Binance rests only on a general AI trend and a novel laundering pattern, which describes what happened to the money after it left, not how the attacker got in (non sequitur). The size of the haul reflects what was in the wallet as much as the hackers' skill.
what_would_change: A named investigator, Binance's own incident report or law-enforcement findings showing AI-assisted intrusion would lift the AI argument; publishing the on-chain receipts (such as the Bitget commingling) in the article would lift the attribution argument toward strongly supported; an FBI or other government attribution would firm up the North Korea link.

script:
Good evening, I'm Professor Reid, and this is ReFrame. Tonight... BBC News reports: Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack.
BBC News reported this on October 31.
The headline: Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack.
The Lazarus Group, a North Korean hacking unit also known as TraderTraitor, was identified "with high confidence" by TRM Labs, as well as Chainalysis.
Some 80% of stolen assets have been secured, a Binance spokesperson said on Friday, but the rest remains unaccounted for.
Let's grade the headline.
Argument one. It comes from TRM Labs and Chainalysis. The reporter relays it... and does not adopt it.
The reasons. Reason one. TRM Labs and Chainalysis identified the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor, "with high confidence."
Reason two. TRM said it's likely the attacker gained access to Binance's hot wallet signing system.
Reason three. Last year, the FBI said North Korea was responsible for the theft of 1.5 billion dollars on the Bybit exchange.
Therefore... A North Korean state-backed group is the likely culprit in the 6.3 billion dollars hack of Binance.
Valid? No.
Cogent? Yes.
Supported? Partly.
Any fallacies? None found.
That's a B.
Why B? Credit where it is earned: two independent firms, a stated confidence level, the hedge word 'likely', and a documented prior case.
But the page never shows what the firms saw.
Chainalysis's own write-up cites stolen Binance funds commingling on-chain with funds from last month's Bitget theft; that receipt never makes the article.
'Robust intelligence' is a description, not the evidence.
Argument two. It comes from Lily Jamali, BBC North America Technology correspondent.
The reasons. Reason one. Experts say the rise of artificial intelligence has also given threat actors new ways to carry out crime, through automation and other means.
Reason two. As Chainalysis put it, the attacker used laundering patterns "we have not seen before".
Therefore... In this case, it's plausible that AI was used to infiltrate Binance's systems.
Valid? No.
Cogent? No.
Supported? No.
Any fallacies? Yes. One: non sequitur.
That's a D.
The fallacy in argument two... non sequitur.
Here's the line. Quote... In this case, it's plausible that AI was used to infiltrate Binance's systems.
Why does it fail here? The only case-specific evidence offered is about laundering, what happened to the money after it left. It says nothing about how the attacker got in. A general trend about AI plus a novel laundering pattern does not lead to AI-assisted infiltration.
Why D? No named expert, firm or investigator in the piece says AI was used to break in.
Binance's own account is a compromised laptop and 'additional points of breach.' 'Plausible' is doing all the work, and nothing on the page carries it.
Argument three. It comes from Lily Jamali, BBC North America Technology correspondent.
The reasons. Reason one. Last year, the FBI said North Korea was responsible for the theft of 1.5 billion dollars on the Bybit exchange.
Reason two. North Korean hackers are also suspected in the theft of 620 million dollars worth of cryptocurrency in 2022.
Reason three. At 6.3 billion dollars, the Binance theft is a record-making heist.
Therefore... If the accusations are true, the heist shows how powerful suspected North Korean hackers have become, a sign that the tools of the hacking trade have grown sharper.
Valid? No.
Cogent? Yes.
Supported? Partly.
Any fallacies? None found.
That's a B-minus.
Why B minus? Fairly hedged: 'if the accusations are true' keeps the attribution conditional, and the rising totals are real reported figures.
But the size of a haul measures what was in the wallet and how it was guarded as much as the thief's skill, and the article itself reports Binance found 'additional points of breach.' Bigger loot is a clue to sharper tools, not proof.
Now, the whole scorecard. Every term here is explained in our grading legend, How We Rate.
Valid: 0 percent.
Cogent: 67 percent.
Conclusion supported: 33 percent.
Fallacy-free: 80 percent.
Overall... a C-plus.
In one line: The attribution is relayed with care; the AI angle is a guess riding on a laundering quote.
Three arguments. Zero valid. Two cogent. None fully supported. One fallacy.
Don't just read the news. ReFrame it.

read: The 20,000 figure is a federal list of registered voters flagged as 'likely' noncitizens, not votes shown to be illegal, and the court ruled against setting those ballots aside, not against fixing proven fraud. title: How We Rate: The Grading Legend with Professor Reid
claim: How We Rate: The Grading Legend with Professor Reid
read: Professor Reid's guide to every ReFrame grade: what valid, cogent and supported mean, the fallacies the show flags most, how a truth table finds a counterexample, how the scorecard is computed and what each letter grade means. Watch it once; every story video after it just gives the grade.

sources.title: ReFrame the Facts with Professor Reid — The Grading Legend (video)

script:
Good evening, I'm Professor Reid, and this is ReFrame. Tonight, no headline. Tonight... how we grade.
This is the guide to every grade on ReFrame. Watch it once... and every story video after it will make sense.
We grade the reasoning, not the politics. An argument is reasons, called premises... offered for a conclusion. We find the main ones, and say who makes each.
We judge only what's on the page. And a reporter who just quotes a claim isn't blamed for it.
Question one. Is it valid? If the reasons are true... must the conclusion be true?
All senators are elected. Ana is a senator. So, Ana is elected. That's valid.
Crime fell after a new law, so the law cut crime? Invalid. Something else could explain the drop.
Question two. Is it cogent? Are the reasons believable, given the evidence... and do they make the conclusion likely?
A signed memo and three named officials? Cogent. One anonymous post? Weak.
Question three. Is it supported? Does the article show the evidence... or just say it exists?
Strong: the evidence is on the page. Partial: some is shown, some only asserted. Unsupported: you're asked to take it on faith.
Question four. Is it fallacy-free? A fallacy is a reasoning trick. It looks like a reason... but it isn't one.
We only name a fallacy when we can quote the line that commits it. And none found... is a perfectly good answer.
Hasty generalization: too few cases, too big a conclusion. Two voters hated the plan... so the whole state does.
Argument from ignorance: no proof, treated as proof. Nobody proved it's safe... so it's dangerous.
Non sequitur: it just doesn't follow. She's a great speaker... so her budget numbers are right.
Begging the question: assuming what you're trying to prove. The report is accurate... because the report says so.
Complex question: a question with a hidden assumption. When will the mayor stop wasting money?
Equivocation: one word, two meanings. A feather is light. Nothing light is dark. So no feather is dark.
The truth table checks validity. P is the reasons. C is the conclusion.
T means true. F means false. Four rows cover every combination.
We hunt for one row: reasons true, conclusion false. Row two.
That's a counterexample. One is enough. Invalid.
To make it valid, add a missing link. If P... then C.
Now, in every row where both premises are true, C is true. No counterexample. Valid.
But is that link actually true? That's what cogent and supported check.
Each argument gets a letter, and so does the whole story.
A: sound and well-evidenced. B: good, with gaps. C: mixed. D: weak. F: no real argument... or seriously fallacious.
Plus and minus place a grade within its letter.
How does it add up? It's a judgment, not a calculator. Each letter weighs all four questions, and the overall grade weighs the arguments.
The percentages show the evidence, so you can check our work. And good reasoning earns an A.
Here's a sample scorecard, with two arguments.
Valid and cogent: the share of arguments that pass. One of two... fifty percent.
Supported: strong counts one, partial a half. Seventy-five.
Fallacy-free: one hundred, minus twenty per fallacy. Eighty.
Below: each argument's grade and four pills. Green, good. Amber, partial. Red, a problem.
Then the final grade. Here... a B-minus.
WHY gives the reason in one line. BY THE NUMBERS counts it up.
From now on, my story videos go straight to the claim, the arguments, any fallacies, the scores... and the grade.
If a term trips you up, come back to How We Rate.
Don't just read the news. ReFrame it.

script:
Good evening, I'm Professor Reid, and this is ReFrame. Tonight... Al Jazeera reports: Argentinian judge drops fraud investigation into Milei over crypto scandal.
Al Jazeera reported this on October 24.
The headline: Argentinian judge drops fraud investigation into Milei over crypto scandal.
President Javier Milei’s role in cryptocurrency launch does not translate into a fraudulent scheme, judge says.
Let's grade the headline.
We ask four questions of every argument.
Is it valid? If the reasons are true... must the conclusion be true?
Is it cogent? Are the reasons believable... and do they make it likely?
Is it supported? Does the article actually show the evidence?
And is it fallacy-free? Does it avoid reasoning tricks... like attacking the person?
Argument one. It comes from Judge Marcelo Martinez de Giorgi. The reporter relays it... and does not adopt it.
The reasons. Reason one. Investor losses and the rise and fall in the Libra price were the core reported events.
Reason two. Those facts are insufficient to establish fraud.
Reason three. Milei's institutional standing may have given the launch greater impact when he posted about it.
Reason four. Greater promotional impact does not by itself amount to a fraudulent scheme.
Reason five. An unstated reason, one we supply: A criminal fraud offence requires a fraudulent scheme — deceit — not market loss or amplification alone.
Therefore... The reported events do not constitute a criminal offence, so the investigation is properly dropped.
Argument one was graded valid. On the board, it has this shape. P... and if P, then C.
Here's every combination of true and false.
Look at every row where both premises are true. C is true every time. No counterexample.
That's what valid means. But valid isn't the same as true. Whether the reasons are true... is what cogent and supported measure.
Is it valid? Yes. If the reasons are true, the conclusion must be true.
Is it cogent? Yes. The reasons are believable and make the conclusion likely.
Is it supported? Partly. Some of it is shown. Some is only asserted.
Any fallacies? None found.
That's a B-plus.
Why B plus? This is real legal reasoning, and it earns the credit.
A crash plus a loud post is not, without more, a fraud; the unstated element of deceit is the obvious one every criminal statute already carries.
I withhold the A only because the text never shows the ruling answering the deleted post, the later denial, or the adviser sitting on near 100 million dollars.
Argument two. It comes from the official presidential office. The reporter relays it... and does not adopt it.
The reasons. Reason one. A president was investigated with complete freedom.
Reason two. The judge ended the inquiry and found no criminal offence.
Therefore... The investigation produced absolute proof of Milei's innocence and was a failed institutional coup that wasted taxpayers' money and the president's time.
Let's put argument two on the board. P stands for its reasons, all together. C is the conclusion.
Here's every combination of true and false.
Row two. The reasons are true... but the conclusion is false. Nothing in the reasons rules that out.
That's a counterexample. One is enough. The argument is invalid.
Is it valid? No. The reasons could all be true and the conclusion still false.
Is it cogent? No. The reasons don't make the conclusion likely.
Is it supported? No. The article doesn't show the evidence.
Any fallacies? Yes. Two: argument from ignorance, and complex question.
That's an F.
The first fallacy in argument two... argument from ignorance.
Here's the line. Quote... For the first time in history, a President of the Nation was investigated with complete freedom, resulting in absolute proof of his innocence
What is argument from ignorance? Treating a lack of proof as if it were proof.
Why does it fail here? A closed inquiry means the charge was not proved. It does not follow that innocence was absolutely proved.
The second fallacy in argument two... complex question.
Here's the line. Quote... Who will take responsibility for having wasted Argentine taxpayers’ money and the President of the Nation’s time in a failed attempt at an institutional coup?
What is complex question? A question that smuggles in an assumption nobody has shown.
Why does it fail here? The question presupposes a coup and a waste. Nothing in the ruling, or in this article, establishes either.
Why F? Put plainly, and kindly: the conclusion reaches further than the reasons can carry; the article doesn't show the evidence for it, and argument from ignorance and complex question stand in for the missing steps. A more modest claim would earn a better grade.
'Absolute proof' does not follow from a file that closed, and 'institutional coup' is a charge smuggled in behind a question mark.
Argument three. It comes from President Javier Milei. The reporter relays it... and does not adopt it.
The reasons. Reason one. He said he had acted in good faith.
Reason two. He accused political rivals of trying to exploit the crash.
Therefore... His promotion of the token was not wrongful; the controversy is political exploitation rather than misconduct.
Is it valid? No. The reasons could all be true and the conclusion still false.
Is it cogent? No. The reasons don't make the conclusion likely.
Is it supported? No. The article doesn't show the evidence.
Any fallacies? None found.
That's a D.
Why D? Relayed, not adopted, and still thin.
'Good faith' is a mental state, and this text offers no evidence of it — only the assertion, plus a finger pointed at rivals.
Weak, not wicked.
Now, the whole scorecard.
Valid: 33 percent.
Cogent: 33 percent.
Conclusion supported: 17 percent.
Fallacy-free: 60 percent. Two fallacies... twenty points each.
Overall... a B.
